source.title: Neural scaling laws from large-N field theory: solvable model beyond the ridgeless limit

record.tranche_reason: Analytically solves a stylized random-feature regression model and derives its test-loss scaling, addressing the general scaling-law question by a different method. It does not test language-model pretraining cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports analytical results for a generative-data, random-feature linear regression model trained with squared loss. It does not measure language-model cross-entropy, training-token or compute scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture shape effects, or downstream task performance. Cited empirical scaling-law results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is an analytical solution of a stylized random-feature linear regression model (Maloney–Roberts–Sully) trained with ridge-regularized squared loss. Its 'scaling laws' are for expected test loss in that toy model. It does not measure language-model pretraining cross-entropy, compute or token scaling, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, other modalities or regimes, or downstream tasks. The record's 'tests'/T2 is inconsistent with its own finding that every version is not tested. The results concern a related but different construct and belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors fully solve the Maloney–Roberts–Sully random-feature model for arbitrary ridge γ and recover the ridgeless result. They derive optimal-loss scaling with corrections to the earlier fit formula, plus new scaling laws for the optimal ridge parameter. They explain N/T symmetry via a diagram-level duality and expect representation learning to break that duality, giving unequal exponents.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a large-N field-theory calculation for a generative-data, random-feature regression model with squared loss and ridge regularization, rather than empirical language-model pretraining-loss sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curves and formulas depend on the latent data spectrum exponent α, the relative sizes N and T, and the ridge parameter γ; the ridgeless limit is singular at N = T.

fits_no_version.finding: In the solvable random-feature model with power-law data spectrum, optimal-ridge test loss scales roughly as (1/N+1/T)^α, with non-trivial corrections when N~T and α≠1. It is ~N^-α for N≪T and plateaus for N≫T. In the ridgeless limit it shows double descent, which optimal γ removes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In solvable random-feature regression, optimally regularized test loss follows a power law then plateau in feature count, with exponent set by the data-spectrum exponent.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal ridge parameter scales roughly as (1/N+1/T)^(α-1), i.e. ~N^(1-α) for N≪T, plateauing for N≫T. It is approximately constant at α=1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal ridge parameter in solvable random-feature regression follows a power-law-then-plateau dependence on model and data size.

fits_no_version.finding: Without label noise the expected test loss is exactly symmetric in N and T (identical exponents), explained by a diagram-level duality. Label noise breaks the symmetry (App. A).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature–sample duality in random-feature models yields equal parameter and data scaling exponents; label noise or representation learning may break it.

record.problems: The evidence is analytical for a simplified random-feature regression model, not an empirical test on language models. The scaling approximations rely on a power-law latent-data spectrum; the text notes that the continuum approximation error can be significant when α ≪ 1. Numerical curves are also shown, but no uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss; only expected squared test loss of a linear random-feature model in the infinite-compute limit.
No extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
No compute-optimal N/T split; only the optimal ridge parameter.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer settings.
No comparison of fitting choices or published exponents in real models.

missing.what: N↔T symmetry of the expected test loss (identical scaling exponents for features and samples) and its breaking by label noise. These are toy-model results not tied to any version.
missing.locator: Sec. III G Eq. (93); Sec. V; App. A Eq. (A15)

record.verdict_notes: This is a theory paper on a toy model, with no empirical language-model or other-modality scaling, so no verdicts are given. The rows are well extracted as toy-model results; all are correctly linked to 'none'.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures expected squared test loss in a stylized regression model, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of larger language-model runs.
The study optimizes a ridge parameter, not the parameter-count/token allocation at fixed compute.
No depth, width, or other architecture comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study does not test image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.

The study derives results for one specified stylized model; it does not compare fitting choices or published language-model scaling exponents. Its toy-model curve shape is recorded under fits_no_version.
